passages.text:
| The United Nations designated Yellowstone National Park as a World Heritage Site and Biosphere Reserve in recognition of the worldwide significance of its natural and cultural resources. These designations do not affect how Yellowstone is managed—the United States retains full jurisdiction over the World Heritage and Biosphere Reserve sites and any related management decisions. World Heritage Site Yellowstone National Park was designated as a World Heritage Site in 1978—the United States' first World Heritage location. This designation is part of the World Heritage Convention international treaty, through which member nations agree to cooperate in the conservation and protection of their cultural and natural heritage sites, and particularly those that have been determined to possess outstanding universal value. The United States was the first nation to sign the World Heritage Convention Treaty; since, 190 other countries have also become members to the agreement. Learn more about the World Heritage Convention. Yellowstone National Park must report regularly to the World Heritage Committee on the status of the park's cultural and natural resources, threats to these resources, and progress made to reduce or eliminate threats. In 1995, the Committee, with the agreement of the United States, placed Yellowstone on its List of World Heritage in Danger. This action was taken in response to specific threats identified to the outstanding universal value of the park. In July 2003, the Committee decided to remove the park from the Danger List. Biosphere Reserve Yellowstone is designated as a biosphere reserve. Biosphere reserves are internationally recognized areas where management seeks to achieve sustainable use of natural resources while ensuring conservation of the biological diversity of the areas. The first biosphere reserves were designated in 1976. On October 26, 1976, United Nations designation of Yellowstone as a biosphere reserve stated:   Yellowstone National Park also reports regularly to United Nations’ Man and the Biosphere Program on the status of the Biosphere Reserve. |

passages.heading: List of World Heritage Sites by year of inscription
passages.text: The United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) designates World Heritage Sites of outstanding universal value to cultural or natural heritage which have been nominated by countries which are signatories to the UNESCO World Heritage Convention, established in 1972.<sup>[1]</sup> Cultural heritage consists of monuments (such as architectural works, monumental sculptures, or inscriptions), groups of buildings, and sites (including archaeological sites). Natural features (consisting of physical and biological formations), geological and physiographical formations (including habitats of threatened species of animals and plants), and natural sites which are important from the point of view of science, conservation or natural beauty, are defined as natural heritage.<sup>[2]</sup> To make a country's historical sites eligible for designation as a World Heritage Sites, the country needs to sign the World Heritage Convention.<sup>[3]</sup> World Heritage Sites are selected during the annual sessions of the World Heritage Committee.<sup>[4]</sup><sup>[5]</sup> The first World Heritage Site in the list is the Galápagos Islands.<sup>[6]</sup> The 24th session in 2000 inscribed the most with 61 entries, while the 13th session in 1989 only inscribed seven sites.<sup>[5]</sup>

passages.heading: Galápagos Islands
passages.text: With the growing importance of ecotourism to the local economy, the airport modernized in the 2010s, using recycled materials for any expansion and shifting entirely to renewable energy sources to handle its roughly 300,000 visitors each year.

passages.heading: History / Pre-Columbian era
passages.text: Whether Polynesians or the indigenous peoples of South America ever made it to the islands is disputed. Oceanic Pacific islands in the same general area as Galápagos—including Clipperton, Cocos, the Desventuradas, the Juan Fernández Islands, and the Revillagigedos—were all uninhabited when discovered by Europeans, with no evidence to indicate any prehistoric human activity.<sup>[45]</sup><sup>[46]</sup><sup>[47]</sup> The easternmost oceanic island in the South Pacific that was discovered with a human population was Easter Island,<sup>[46]</sup> whose Rapa Nui people are known to be Polynesian rather than South American.<sup>[48]</sup>

passages.heading: 20th century
passages.text: Galápagos National Park was established in 1959,<sup>[86]</sup> with tourism starting to expand in the 1960s, imposing several restrictions upon the human population already living on the island. However, opportunities in the tourism, fishing, and farming industries attracted a mass of poor fishermen and farmers from mainland Ecuador. In the 1990s and 2000s, violent confrontations between parts of the local population and the Galápagos National Park Service occurred, including capturing and killing giant tortoises and holding staff of the Galápagos National Park Service hostage to obtain higher annual sea cucumber quotas.<sup>[87]</sup>

passages.heading: Environmental protection policy
passages.text: In 1986, the 70,000 square kilometers (27,000 sq mi) of ocean surrounding the islands was declared a marine reserve, second in size only to Australia's Great Barrier Reef. In 1990, the archipelago became a whale sanctuary. UNESCO recognized the islands in 1978 as a World Heritage Site<sup>[104]</sup> and in 1985, as a biosphere reserve. This was later extended in December 2001 to include the marine reserve. In July 2010, the World Heritage Committee agreed to remove the Galápagos Islands from its list of precious sites endangered by environmental threats or overuse.<sup>[105]</sup>

passages.heading: Environmental threats
passages.text: Introduced plants and animals, such as feral goats, cats, and cattle, brought accidentally or willingly to the islands by humans, represent the main threat to Galápagos.<sup>[107]</sup> Quick to reproduce and with no natural predators, these alien species decimated the habitats of native species. The native animals, lacking natural predators on the islands, are defenseless to introduced predators.

passages.heading: Environmental threats
passages.text:
In 2007, UNESCO put the Galápagos Islands on their List of World Heritage in Danger because of threats posed by invasive species, unbridled tourism and overfishing.<sup>[117]</sup>
On 29 July 2010, the World Heritage Committee decided to remove the Galápagos Islands from the list because the Committee found significant progress had been made by Ecuador in addressing these problems.<sup>[118]</sup>

On 28 January 2008, Galápagos National Park official Victor Carrion announced 53 sea lions (13 pups, 25 youngsters, 9 males and 6 females) were killed at the Galápagos Islands nature reserve on Pinta, with their heads caved in. In 2001, poachers killed 35 male sea lions.<sup>[119]</sup>

passages.heading: Description
passages.text: The HMR is located within Ecuador’s Insular Exclusive Economic Zone (IEEZ), northeast of Galápagos Islands, and constitutes a marine ecosystem of critical importance due to its unparalleled biodiversity and ecological significance. The HMR encompasses seamounts and pelagic environments that are essential for the life cycles and migration of threatened species associated with the Galapagos Marine Reserve (GMR) and the Galápagos National Park (GNP), including the hammerhead shark (Sphyrna spp.) and the leatherback turtle (Dermochelys coriacea), among others. The HMR therefore plays a crucial role in maintaining the integrity of the property by ensuring the conservation of endangered species and the preservation of unique marine ecosystems with intrinsic value as natural heritage of outstanding significance.

passages.heading: Description
passages.text: With an area of 6,000,000 ha (MAATE, 2023), the inclusion of the Hermandad Marine Reserve in Galápagos Islands – with a total area of 14,066,514 ha comprising the Galápagos National Park (GNP) and the Galápagos Marine Reserve (GMR) – strengthens the protection of the Outstanding Universal Value (OUV) by enhancing connectivity for migratory species across the region.

passages.heading: Statements of authenticity and/or integrity
passages.text: Under the Organic Environmental Code (CODA) and its General Implementing Regulations (RCODA), the administration of the HMR is non-delegable and rests with the MAATE. However, due to its importance and the type of threats to which it is exposed, the property is supported by an inter-institutional framework where different actors are articulated through Interministerial Agreement No. MAATE-MND-MEF-MPCEIP-MREMH-002-2023, demonstrating Ecuador's commitment to marine conservation within the jurisdiction of each State Department involved.

passages.heading: Statements of authenticity and/or integrity
passages.text: The governance and administration of the Hermandad Marine Reserve, the Galapagos Marine Reserve, and the Galapagos National Park are the responsibility of the latter. This ensures the proper management, supervision, and coordination of the three PAs that comprise the Galapagos Islands site. Additionally, the reserve has been included in the National System of Protected Areas (SNAP) under an ecosystem and regional approach that focuses on the importance of connectivity and national and global cooperation to achieve conservation and sustainable use objectives.

passages.heading: Comparison with other similar properties
passages.text: Currently, the World Heritage List (UNESCO, 2025) includes a total of 51 marine reserves, representing 4.3% of the inscribed properties. The expansion of the Galapagos Islands with the addition of the Hermandad Marine Reserve stands out as a benchmark for biodiversity and marine conservation globally, especially in the context of the ETP.

Oceanic Pacific islands in the same general area as Galápagos—including Clipperton, Cocos, the Desventuradas, the Juan Fernández Islands, and the Revillagigedos—were all uninhabited when discovered by Europeans, with no evidence to indicate any prehistoric human activity.<sup>[45]</sup><sup>[46]</sup><sup>[47]</sup> The easternmost oceanic island in the South Pacific that was discovered with a human population was Easter Island,<sup>[46]</sup> whose Rapa Nui people are known to be Polynesian rather than South American.<sup>[48]</sup>

Section: 20th century
Galápagos National Park was established in 1959,<sup>[86]</sup> with tourism starting to expand in the 1960s, imposing several restrictions upon the human population already living on the island. However, opportunities in the tourism, fishing, and farming industries attracted a mass of poor fishermen and farmers from mainland Ecuador. In the 1990s and 2000s, violent confrontations between parts of the local population and the Galápagos National Park Service occurred, including capturing and killing giant tortoises and holding staff of the Galápagos National Park Service hostage to obtain higher annual sea cucumber quotas.<sup>[87]</sup>

Section: Environmental protection policy
In 1986, the 70,000 square kilometers (27,000 sq mi) of ocean surrounding the islands was declared a marine reserve, second in size only to Australia's Great Barrier Reef. In 1990, the archipelago became a whale sanctuary. UNESCO recognized the islands in 1978 as a World Heritage Site<sup>[104]</sup> and in 1985, as a biosphere reserve. This was later extended in December 2001 to include the marine reserve. In July 2010, the World Heritage Committee agreed to remove the Galápagos Islands from its list of precious sites endangered by environmental threats or overuse.<sup>[105]</sup>

Section: Environmental threats
Introduced plants and animals, such as feral goats, cats, and cattle, brought accidentally or willingly to the islands by humans, represent the main threat to Galápagos.<sup>[107]</sup> Quick to reproduce and with no natural predators, these alien species decimated the habitats of native species. The native animals, lacking natural predators on the islands, are defenseless to introduced predators.

Section: Environmental threats
In 2007, UNESCO put the Galápagos Islands on their List of World Heritage in Danger because of threats posed by invasive species, unbridled tourism and overfishing.<sup>[117]</sup>
On 29 July 2010, the World Heritage Committee decided to remove the Galápagos Islands from the list because the Committee found significant progress had been made by Ecuador in addressing these problems.<sup>[118]</sup>

On 28 January 2008, Galápagos National Park official Victor Carrion announced 53 sea lions (13 pups, 25 youngsters, 9 males and 6 females) were killed at the Galápagos Islands nature reserve on Pinta, with their heads caved in. In 2001, poachers killed 35 male sea lions.<sup>[119]</sup>

Section: Description
The HMR is located within Ecuador’s Insular Exclusive Economic Zone (IEEZ), northeast of Galápagos Islands, and constitutes a marine ecosystem of critical importance due to its unparalleled biodiversity and ecological significance. The HMR encompasses seamounts and pelagic environments that are essential for the life cycles and migration of threatened species associated with the Galapagos Marine Reserve (GMR) and the Galápagos National Park (GNP), including the hammerhead shark (Sphyrna spp.) and the leatherback turtle (Dermochelys coriacea), among others. The HMR therefore plays a crucial role in maintaining the integrity of the property by ensuring the conservation of endangered species and the preservation of unique marine ecosystems with intrinsic value as natural heritage of outstanding significance.

Section: Description
With an area of 6,000,000 ha (MAATE, 2023), the inclusion of the Hermandad Marine Reserve in Galápagos Islands – with a total area of 14,066,514 ha comprising the Galápagos National Park (GNP) and the Galápagos Marine Reserve (GMR) – strengthens the protection of the Outstanding Universal Value (OUV) by enhancing connectivity for migratory species across the region.

Section: Statements of authenticity and/or integrity
Under the Organic Environmental Code (CODA) and its General Implementing Regulations (RCODA), the administration of the HMR is non-delegable and rests with the MAATE. However, due to its importance and the type of threats to which it is exposed, the property is supported by an inter-institutional framework where different actors are articulated through Interministerial Agreement No. MAATE-MND-MEF-MPCEIP-MREMH-002-2023, demonstrating Ecuador's commitment to marine conservation within the jurisdiction of each State Department involved.

Section: Statements of authenticity and/or integrity
The governance and administration of the Hermandad Marine Reserve, the Galapagos Marine Reserve, and the Galapagos National Park are the responsibility of the latter. This ensures the proper management, supervision, and coordination of the three PAs that comprise the Galapagos Islands site. Additionally, the reserve has been included in the National System of Protected Areas (SNAP) under an ecosystem and regional approach that focuses on the importance of connectivity and national and global cooperation to achieve conservation and sustainable use objectives.

Section: Comparison with other similar properties
Currently, the World Heritage List (UNESCO, 2025) includes a total of 51 marine reserves, representing 4.3% of the inscribed properties. The expansion of the Galapagos Islands with the addition of the Hermandad Marine Reserve stands out as a benchmark for biodiversity and marine conservation globally, especially in the context of the ETP.
